channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: UK unemployment fell to 4.7% in the three months to August from 4.9%, while vacancies fell by 21,000 to 691,000 in the three months to September, the lowest in over five years, with the largest decrease in construction, the ONS reports.
item.description:
The Guardian and MarketScreener report ONS figures showing that the UK unemployment rate was 4.7% in the three months to August, down from 4.9% in the three months to July, and the Guardian says the number of unemployed fell by 47,000 in the quarter to 1.712 million. The BBC reports that there were 691,000 vacancies in the three months to September, 21,000 fewer than in the previous three months and the lowest level in more than five years, that the ONS cited labour costs as a key factor in the fall in vacancies, and that construction recorded the largest decrease in vacancies. MarketScreener reports that average total earnings growth fell from 3.9% in the three months to July to 3.7% in the three months to August, that growth excluding bonuses rose from 3.6% to 3.7%, that private-sector pay growth rose from 2.9% to 3.0%, the first rise since the end of 2024, and that a preliminary tax-office measure of payrolled employees rose by 13,000 in September. The rows do not give the size of the vacancy fall in construction, the sectors behind the fall in unemployment or a definition of the private-sector pay measure, and the two measures cover different periods, unemployment to August and vacancies to September.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows combine a falling unemployment rate with falling vacancies. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a fall in vacancies, and in construction most of all, can reflect weaker hiring intentions among employers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, construction is a customer group, so weaker hiring in construction could signal slower building activity, although vacancies are one indicator among several. The rows give no figures for construction output or orders. Points that may be worth considering include UK construction output and survey data, the next labour-market release and the size of the construction fall in vacancies.

The Guardian | MarketScreener, unemployment and earnings | MarketScreener, pay and payrolls | BBC News

item.title: Vietnam's registered foreign direct investment rose 76.4% year on year to USD 50.36 billion in January to September, with disbursed capital up 12.1% to USD 21.07 billion, the highest in five years.
item.description:
VietnamPlus reports that registered foreign direct investment into Vietnam rose 76.4% year on year to USD 50.36 billion in January to September 2026, with more than USD 9.7 billion registered in September alone, and that disbursed capital rose 12.1% to USD 21.07 billion, the highest level in five years. The Foreign Investment Agency of the Ministry of Finance says registered FDI could exceed USD 60 billion for the full year and could reach USD 70 billion if several large projects are approved in the fourth quarter, and that disbursed FDI could approach USD 30 billion. The row does not give the sectors or countries of origin behind the increase, the number or size of the large projects, the 2025 base for registered capital the base period for the 12.1% rise in disbursed capital or any effect on output.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives both registered and disbursed capital. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a rise in registered investment of that size can raise factory construction and equipment orders in the following quarters, and disbursement shows how much has been spent. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, new factories use construction adhesive technologies and manufacturing plants use industrial adhesive technologies, so continued growth in disbursed capital could support demand in Vietnam and in supply chains that move production there. The row gives no figure for chemical or materials-intensive sectors. Points that may be worth considering include the sector split of the new projects, the fourth-quarter approvals and the next disbursement data.

VietnamPlus

item.title: Witkoff is to meet Putin on Wednesday after talks with Zelenskyy in Norway on a peace framework, while Trump says other people should negotiate for Ukraine and, the Economic Times reports, proposes a potential trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that Witkoff is to meet Putin on Wednesday after what a US official called constructive talks with Zelenskyy in Norway, which covered key elements of a comprehensive peace framework: security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic plan and a broader European security architecture. The Hong Kong Commercial Daily reports that on 19 October Trump said it was time for other people to negotiate with Russia on Ukraine's behalf and that Zelenskyy should have settled the war long ago, and that he defended his diesel deal with Putin and the easing of sanctions on Russia on the ground that the US is negotiating with Russia and he does not want to disrupt the talks halfway. The Economic Times reports Trump warning that Zelenskyy must commit to negotiating, with severe consequences otherwise, and proposing a potential trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi. Zaobao instead says the Wall Street Journal reported that Putin proposed a trilateral meeting in a call with Trump on 9 October, to be held at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 18–19 November, citing informed former Russian intelligence officials. Daily Sabah reports Zelenskyy saying that Kyiv must be included in any such talks. Politico says Trump does not regard the war as one with fault on both sides and that the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas told the European Parliament that American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for almost two years. The rows give no agenda for the meeting with Putin and no terms for any settlement.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe contacts and statements, not agreed terms. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a settlement or ceasefire would change sanctions, energy trade and the demand for reconstruction, while a break between Washington and Kyiv would add uncertainty about sanctions and support. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, reconstruction would raise demand for construction materials in Ukraine, and changes in sanctions on Russia would affect energy and raw-material prices and trade routes. The rows give no figure for reconstruction needs and no terms for sanctions. Points that may be worth considering include the outcome of the Witkoff–Putin meeting, any agenda for a meeting at the APEC summit, and any change to the easing of sanctions on Russia.

MarketScreener | Hong Kong Commercial Daily | The Economic Times | Lianhe Zaobao | Daily Sabah | Politico

item.title: An Ifo study says Germany's research spending is concentrated in middle-technology sectors, with high-tech fields at 68% of US manufacturing R&D spending in 2023 against a German share of 20%.
item.description:
Anadolu Agency reports an Ifo Institute study in which the researchers Oliver Falck and Yuchen Guo found that Europe's weak economic growth stemmed from an innovation deficit known as the middle-technology trap. According to the report, fast-growing economies concentrated research and development on high-tech sectors such as biotechnology, IT hardware and software and aerospace, while German R&D stayed heavily focused on middle-technology sectors such as machinery and automotive manufacturing, unlike the US and China. High-tech sectors made up 68% of manufacturing R&D spending in the US in 2023, while Germany's share stood at 20%. The report says that shifting spending towards high-tech fields boosts economic growth. The row gives 2023 for the US figure and does not state the year for the German figure. It does not give the Chinese share, the size of the growth effect, the period or method of the study or how it classifies sectors.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row describes one study's comparison of research spending shares and a conclusion about growth that rests on the study's method. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, an industrial base weighted towards machinery and vehicles is exposed to the demand cycles and competition in those sectors, and a shift of research towards other fields would change which industries buy materials. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, machinery and automotive manufacturing are customer groups, so a lasting weight on those sectors keeps demand tied to them, while a shift of investment towards other manufacturing fields could widen the customer base over time. The row gives no figures for chemical or materials research. Points that may be worth considering include the study's data and method, German R&D by sector over time, and how the sectors named in the study use adhesive technologies.

Anadolu Agency

item.title: Taiwan's export orders grew 62.4% year on year to USD 114.21 billion in September, the second month above USD 100 billion, with demand for AI, high-performance computing and cloud services cited as the driver.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs said on 20 October that export orders reached USD 114.21 billion in September, 62.4% above a year earlier and the second consecutive month above USD 100 billion, and says the growth was attributed to demand for AI, high-performance computing and cloud services. Orders from the US, Europe and Japan rose 79.4%, 68.0% and 35.5%. Orders for electronic products rose 71.0%, and orders for the second category, which MarketScreener calls telecoms products and Commercial Times calls information and communication products, rose 87.3%. The ministry expects October orders to be 62.0% to 67.0% higher than a year earlier and says full-year orders could reach USD 1.1 trillion. Commercial Times adds that orders for January to September were USD 819.2 billion, 56% more than a year earlier and above the USD 743 billion for all of 2025, that the statistics director said strong demand and prices for new consumer electronics exceeded the department's forecasts, and that orders for optical instruments fell 5.6% on a slowdown in customer pull-in and conservative panel demand. The rows do not state the comparison period for the regional, product and optical-instrument figures, do not separate price from volume, give the share of AI products or say where the ordered goods are produced.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows measure orders received, and the statistics director's remark on prices for new consumer electronics suggests that part of the growth reflects prices. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, orders come before shipments and production, and growth driven by AI servers and electronics raises demand for components, materials and production capacity in the electronics supply chain. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, electronics assembly and semiconductor packaging use adhesive technologies, so strong order growth could point to higher demand from electronics customers, with the effect depending on how much of the growth is volume rather than price. The rows give no figures for materials spending. Points that may be worth considering include shipment data, the ministry's October figure and orders for products outside AI.

MarketScreener | Commercial Times, September orders | Commercial Times, January to September

item.title: A John Burns survey cited by the Wall Street Journal finds two-thirds of US construction contractors say immigration raids have hurt the housing market, against 13% who said the same in September 2025 and 23% in March 2026.
item.description:
The Independent reports, citing a survey by John Burns Research & Consulting that the Wall Street Journal cited, that two-thirds of US construction contractors believe ICE raids on immigrant communities have had an adverse effect on the housing market by making it harder to find workers and leaving new builds at a standstill. It reports that 13% said the same in September 2025 and 23% in March 2026. The Journal, the row says, suggests that the raids caused worker shortages only in isolated regions such as South Texas last year and that the widening of the net this summer has created a much bigger problem for a sector that has often relied on flexible migrant labour for roofers, painters and framers. Scott Brannock, president of the Northeast Florida Builders Association, says framers' pay rose to USD 45 an hour from USD 20 as a result of the sudden worker shortage and that framing labour now accounts for USD 28,000 of the cost of building a 2,500-square-foot house, against USD 10,000 before. The row does not give the survey's sample size, dates or base, does not say whether the 13% and 23% were measured on the same group of respondents (it calls the two-thirds contractors and the earlier shares builders), and gives no figure for starts or build times attributable to the raids.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row combines survey shares with figures from one builder-association president, so it describes reported pressure on labour supply and cost, not measured building volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a shortage of site workers can slow completions and raise building costs, and costs that rise faster than prices can reduce builders' willingness to start projects. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, flooring, insulation and wall and roof installation use adhesive technologies, so a labour-constrained sector could install more slowly and, in some cases, show more interest in products that shorten installation time, while lower completions would lower demand. The row gives no figure for the share of building sites affected. Points that may be worth considering include later survey rounds, starts and completions data, and builders' reports on labour costs.

The Independent

item.title: China's hybrid car exports to the EU grew 204.2% year on year in September to almost 100,000 units, and Morgan Stanley says Chinese carmakers are preparing more local production as they face an EU import quota.
item.description:
The South China Morning Post reports, citing customs data, that China's hybrid car exports to the EU grew 204.2% in September 2026 compared with September 2025, to almost 100,000 units, higher than the 142.7% growth in passenger car exports to the EU, for which the row gives no period. In two further rows it reports Morgan Stanley analysts saying that Chinese carmakers are preparing more local production as they face an EU import quota targeting hybrid vehicles: they plan to use idle plants of international brands or to invest billions of yuan in their own factories, which the analysts say would favour Chinese EV leaders with the scale, balance sheets and European manufacturing plans already under way. The second row says the analysts' note followed an agreement between Beijing and Brussels on an import quota for Chinese-made hybrid vehicles and describes a shift from exporting vehicles to producing them locally and from price-led share gains to margin-led positioning. The rows do not give the size or start date of the quota, the number of vehicles it covers, the 2025 base in units, the brands or plants involved or the share of the EU market that the exports represent.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows combine one customs figure with analysts' views of company plans, not announced investments. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a quota that limits imports together with more local assembly would move production of vehicles for Europe from China to Europe, and competition between exporters could shift from price to margin. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle assembly and electric-vehicle batteries use adhesive technologies, so more assembly in Europe could change where those products are bought and qualified, while the fast growth of imports in the meantime keeps part of the demand tied to Chinese plants. The rows give no figures for European assembly capacity or supplier choices. Points that may be worth considering include the quota's terms, announcements of plant locations, and European market-share data for Chinese brands.

South China Morning Post, hybrid exports | South China Morning Post, local production | South China Morning Post, Morgan Stanley note

item.title: Merz says investors have so far pledged about EUR 230 billion at the first investment summit and Made for Germany companies plan over EUR 800 billion by 2028; Bild says it is unclear how much was secured at the conference.
item.description:
Süddeutsche Zeitung and Handelsblatt report that Chancellor Merz said at the federal government's first investment summit that investors had so far pledged around EUR 230 billion, citing Amazon's plan to invest around EUR 16 billion in Germany; Bild says the Amazon investment is for 2027. Handelsblatt says around 200 international and German chief executives took part. Süddeutsche Zeitung also names Nvidia, Schwarz Group, RWE, Blackstone, Microsoft and Sanofi and says the corporate Made for Germany initiative intends to invest more than EUR 800 billion in Germany by 2028; Bild adds that the initiative, launched about a year ago, originally announced EUR 631 billion. A second Bild row says it is unclear how many of the billions were actually secured at the conference and that two deals are certain, Amazon and Nvidia. Anadolu says the planned investments cover automation, robotics, defence, optics, photonics, fusion technology, quantum computing and health, and that Merz said the government will continue tax relief for investing companies, work for cheaper and more reliable energy and cut red tape. The rows give the economics ministry's figure differently: Handelsblatt says the ministry named EUR 228.6 billion as the total volume of the largest investment projects in Germany in 2026 alone, of which EUR 95.5 billion came from foreign companies, across more than 70 projects each above EUR 100 million, while Tagesschau quotes Economics Minister Reiche on commitments of EUR 228 billion that include only projects above EUR 100 million and Bild quotes her on over EUR 220 billion. The rows do not say how the EUR 230 billion, the EUR 800 billion and the EUR 228.6 billion relate to each other, what share is new or when the money would be spent.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report pledges and project volumes, not investment flows or orders. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, announced investment turns into construction and equipment orders only in part and with a lag, and the areas named, such as data centres, logistics and industrial automation, are capital-intensive. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, new plants, data centres and logistics buildings use construction and industrial adhesive technologies, so pledges that become projects could add demand with a delay, while pledges that are not realised would not. The rows give no figure for the chemical or construction sectors. Points that may be worth considering include how much of the total is new rather than already planned, the start dates of named projects, and the next direct-investment data.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | Handelsblatt | Bild, EUR 800 billion | Bild, secured amounts | Anadolu Agency | Tagesschau

item.title: US single-family housing starts fell 4.6% in September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 859,000, which MarketScreener calls the lowest since September 2025, and single-family permits fell 4.0% to a rate of 845,000, the Census Bureau says.
item.description:
The Standard reports, citing the Census Bureau of the Commerce Department, that US single-family housing starts fell 4.6% in September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 859,000 units and that single-family building permits fell 4.0% to a rate of 845,000 units. MarketScreener's summary gives the same starts figure, calls it the lowest level since September 2025, and says single-family starts were 2.6% higher than a year earlier. The rows do not state the month against which the 4.6% fall is measured, and do not say whether the 4.0% fall in permits is also measured against the previous month. They give no figures for multi-family housing, total starts, completions or homes under construction, no regional breakdown and no explanation for the fall.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows cover single-family starts and permits only. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, starts lead the use of building materials by some months, so a lower annual rate points to lower volumes later, and permits below starts suggest the pipeline is not widening. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, new houses use adhesive technologies in insulation, flooring and facades, so a lower starts rate could lower demand from US residential construction, while the year-on-year gain shows that the level is still above that of a year earlier. The rows give no figures for multi-family building. Points that may be worth considering include multi-family and total starts, completions, and the October data.

The Standard | MarketScreener

item.title: Wallstreet:online reports that German producer prices rose 6.7% year on year in September, the strongest rise since March 2023, and 1.9% from August, with energy prices up 14.9% year on year.
item.description:
Wallstreet:online reports that producer prices in Germany accelerated surprisingly strongly in September: they were 6.7% above the previous year's level, the strongest increase since March 2023, and 1.9% above August. It names energy prices as the main driver, up 14.9% year on year, and says mineral oil products became particularly more expensive. The row does not name the statistical office that published the figures, does not say which product groups the index covers and does not give the forecast it surprised. It gives no figure for producer prices excluding energy, no breakdown beyond mineral oil products and no figure for chemical products.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives a headline producer-price figure for Germany. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a rise in producer prices of this size can pass into the costs of downstream manufacturers with a delay, and an energy-led rise adds to operating costs for energy-intensive producers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, energy and mineral oil products are inputs to the chemical industry, so higher prices could raise the cost of raw materials and of production in Germany, with the effect depending on contract terms and on how much producers pass on. The row gives no figure for chemical products. Points that may be worth considering include the producer-price index excluding energy, the October release, and whether prices for chemical products follow energy.

Wallstreet:online
